summary.text: The proof constructs the two natural candidates from the totient formulas and uses \(\varphi(m)<m\) for a baseline lower bound, then excludes every integer in the remaining gap. Its key classification shows that an odd number with power-of-two totient is a product of distinct Fermat primes; uniqueness of sums of distinct powers of two forces the only possible odd exception to be the relevant Fermat number, while separating the power of two from the odd part gives the stronger bound for every even candidate.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_{>0}:2^n\mid \varphi(m)\},
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. We prove the following statement, which is slightly more general than the assertion for \(33\): for every nonnegative integer \(K\), if
\[
N=2^K\qquad\text{and}\qquad F_K=2^{2^K}+1=2^N+1,
\]
then
\[
A(N)=
\begin{cases}
F_K,&F_K\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
2^{N+1},&F_K\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]
Taking \(K=33\) gives exactly the desired result.

We begin with the structural fact about odd numbers whose totient is a power of two that will be needed in the nonprime case.

**Classification lemma.** If \(q\) is odd and
\[
\varphi(q)=2^s,
\]
then there is a finite set \(T\) of nonnegative integers such that
\[
q=\prod_{j\in T}F_j,
\qquad F_j=2^{2^j}+1\text{ is prime for every }j\in T,
\qquad s=\sum_{j\in T}2^j.
\]
In particular, the Fermat primes appearing in the product are distinct.

We prove this by induction on \(q\). If \(q=1\), then \(\varphi(q)=1\), so \(2^s=1\), whence \(s=0\). The assertion holds with \(T\) empty.

Now suppose \(q>1\), and let \(p\) be a prime divisor of \(q\). Write
\[
q=p^e r,
\]
where \(e\geq 1\) and \(p\nmid r\). Thus \(p^e\) and \(r\) are coprime. Since \(q\) is odd, \(p\) is an odd prime. Multiplicativity of the totient on coprime factors and the prime-power formula for the totient give
\[
2^s=\varphi(q)=\varphi(p^e)\varphi(r)
=p^{e-1}(p-1)\varphi(r).
\]
If \(e\geq 2\), then \(p\) divides the right-hand side and hence divides \(2^s\). The only prime divisor of \(2^s\) is \(2\), contradicting the fact that \(p\) is odd. Therefore \(e=1\), and
\[
2^s=(p-1)\varphi(r).
\]
It follows that \(p-1\) divides \(2^s\). Every positive divisor of a power of \(2\) is a power of \(2\), so
\[
p-1=2^t
\]
for some \(t\leq s\). As \(p\) is odd and at least \(3\), we have \(t>0\).

We next use the elementary fact that if \(2^t+1\) is prime, then \(t\) is a power of \(2\). Indeed, write \(t=2^j u\), where \(u\) is odd. If \(u>1\), then with \(x=2^{2^j}>1\),
\[
2^t+1=x^u+1

after setting \(x=2^{2^j}\). Since \(u\) is odd,
\[
x^u+1=(x+1)(x^{u-1}-x^{u-2}+\cdots-x+1),
\]
which is a nontrivial factorization. Thus primality forces \(u=1\), and hence \(t=2^j\) for some \(j\geq0\). Consequently
\[
p=2^t+1=2^{2^j}+1=F_j,
\]
and this Fermat number is prime.

Returning to
\[
2^s=2^t\varphi(r),
\]
and using \(t\leq s\), cancellation gives
\[
\varphi(r)=2^{s-t}=2^{s-2^j}.
\]
The number \(r\) is odd and is strictly smaller than \(q\), so the induction hypothesis applies to it. Thus there is a finite set \(T'\) such that
\[
r=\prod_{i\in T'}F_i,
\qquad F_i\text{ is prime for all }i\in T',
\qquad s-t=\sum_{i\in T'}2^i.
\]
Moreover, \(j\notin T'\), because otherwise \(F_j=p\) would divide \(r\), contrary to the choice of \(r\). Therefore, with \(T=T'\cup\{j\}\),
\[
q=pr=\prod_{i\in T}F_i
\]
and
\[
s=t+(s-t)=2^j+\sum_{i\in T'}2^i=\sum_{i\in T}2^i.
\]
This proves the classification lemma.

We will also use the uniqueness of a sum of distinct powers of two: if \(U\) and \(V\) are finite sets of nonnegative integers and
\[
\sum_{j\in U}2^j=\sum_{j\in V}2^j,
\]
then \(U=V\). One direct proof is to suppose the sets differ and choose the largest index \(d\) belonging to exactly one of them. The contribution \(2^d\) on one side cannot be matched by all smaller powers on the other, because
\[
1+2+\cdots+2^{d-1}=2^d-1<2^d.
\]
This is simply uniqueness of binary expansion. In particular,
\[
\sum_{j\in T}2^j=2^K
\]
forces \(T=\{K\}\).

We now determine \(A(N)\), where \(N=2^K\). First observe that the set defining \(A(N)\) is nonempty. Indeed,
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N,
\]
so \(2^N\mid\varphi(2^{N+1})\). Thus \(2^{N+1}\) is always an admissible value.

Next we establish a preliminary lower bound valid for every admissible \(m\):
\[
m\geq 2^N+1.
\]
Suppose \(m>0\) and \(2^N\mid\varphi(m)\). Since \(N=2^K\geq1\), we have \(2^N\geq2\). The case \(m=1\) is impossible because \(\varphi(1)=1\), which is not divisible by \(2^N\). Hence \(m\geq2\). Since \(\varphi(m)>0\) and is divisible by \(2^N\),
\[
\varphi(m)\geq2^N.
\]
For every \(m\geq2\), \(\varphi(m)<m\), because among the integers from \(1\) to \(m\), the integer \(m\) itself is not coprime to \(m\). Therefore
\[
2^N\leq\varphi(m)<m,
\]
which, as these are integers, gives \(m\geq2^N+1\).

We now split according to the primality of
\[
F_K=2^N+1.
\]

### Prime case

Assume \(F_K\) is prime. Then
\[
\varphi(F_K)=F_K-1=2^N,
\]
so \(F_K\) is admissible. The preliminary lower bound says every admissible positive integer is at least \(2^N+1=F_K\). Hence
\[
A(N)=F_K.
\]

### Nonprime case

Assume \(F_K\) is not prime. Since \(F_K=2^N+1>1\), this is equivalently the composite case. We already know that \(2^{N+1}\) is admissible. It remains to show that no admissible positive integer is smaller than \(2^{N+1}\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(m\) is admissible and
\[
m<2^{N+1}.
\]
The preliminary lower bound gives
\[
2^N+1\leq m<2^{N+1}.
\]
As above,
\[
2^N\leq\varphi(m)<m<2^{N+1}=2\cdot2^N.
\]
Because \(\varphi(m)\) is a multiple of \(2^N\), the only possibility in this interval is
\[
\varphi(m)=2^N.
\]

Factor out the exact power of \(2\) dividing \(m\). Thus write
\[
m=2^a r,
\]
where \(a\geq0\), \(r\) is odd, and \(2^a\) and \(r\) are coprime. We consider separately the cases \(a=0\) and \(a>0\).

#### Subcase 1: \(a=0\)

Then \(m=r\) is odd and
\[
\varphi(r)=2^N.
\]
Apply the classification lemma with exponent \(s=N\). There is a finite set \(T\) such that every \(F_j\) for \(j\in T\) is prime and
\[
N=\sum_{j\in T}2^j.
\]
But \(N=2^K\). By uniqueness of binary expansion,
\[
T=\{K\}.
\]
The classification lemma therefore says, in particular, that \(F_K\) is prime. This contradicts our assumption that \(F_K\) is not prime. Hence an admissible \(m<2^{N+1}\) cannot be odd.

#### Subcase 2: \(a>0\)

Since \(2^a\) and \(r\) are coprime, multiplicativity of the totient and the formula \(\varphi(2^a)=2^{a-1}\) give
\[
2^N=\varphi(m)=2^{a-1}\varphi(r).
\]
We split once more according to whether \(r=1\).

If \(r=1\), then
\[
2^{a-1}=2^N.
\]
Powers of \(2\) have unique exponents, so \(a-1=N\), or \(a=N+1\). Thus
\[
m=2^a=2^{N+1},
\]
contradicting the strict assumption \(m<2^{N+1}\).

It remains to consider \(r>1\). Since \(r\) is odd, this means in particular \(r\geq3\), though only \(r\geq2\) is needed. From
\[
2^{a-1}\varphi(r)=2^N
\]
it follows that \(\varphi(r)\) is itself a power of two. Write
\[
\varphi(r)=2^u.
\]
Comparing powers of two in the preceding equality yields
\[
(a-1)+u=N.
\]
Because \(r\geq2\), the strict totient inequality gives
\[
2^u=\varphi(r)<r,
\]
so
\[
r\geq2^u+1.
\]
Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
m=2^a r
&\geq 2^a(2^u+1)\\
&=2^{a+u}+2^a.
\end{aligned}
\]
But \((a-1)+u=N\), hence \(a+u=N+1\). Therefore
\[
m\geq2^{N+1}+2^a>2^{N+1},
\]
again contradicting \(m<2^{N+1}\).

All possibilities for an admissible \(m<2^{N+1}\) have led to contradictions. Thus every admissible \(m\) satisfies
\[
m\geq2^{N+1}.
\]
Since \(2^{N+1}\) itself is admissible, it follows that in the nonprime case
\[
A(N)=2^{N+1}.
\]

Combining the two cases, for every \(K\geq0\),
\[
A(2^K)=
\begin{cases}
2^{2^K}+1,&2^{2^K}+1\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
2^{2^K+1},&2^{2^K}+1\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]
Finally, setting \(K=33\), so that \(N=2^{33}\) and \(F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1\), gives
\[
A(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
2^{2^{33}+1},&F_{33}\text{ is composite},
\end{cases}
\]
which is the conjectured value.
